name: constmap
workload: Random-order single-key lookups over every key in a 1,000,000-key string-to-uint64 dataset, plus batched get-many lookups.
claimed_speedup: ConstMap 8.7 ns/op vs Go map 46 ns/op (~5.3x) on Apple M4 Max; VerifiedConstMap 15 ns/op (~3.1x); memory ~9.0 bytes/key vs ~48 bytes/key for Go map
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain, go test -bench (benchmark code public in repo: hashbatch_bench_test.go, batch_bench_test.go, paired_test.go)
hardware: Apple M4 Max; also tested on Intel Xeon Gold 6548N for batched comparisons
tradeoffs: Immutable: keys must be known at construction time (build-then-query), so it targets static/compile-time-known key sets like std::unordered_map replacements built from a fixed keyword set, not general dynamic maps. Uses a binary-fuse-filter-style construction (~9 bytes/key) rather than a hash table with separate chaining/open addressing.
caveats: Author's own README explicitly warns the benchmark methodology avoids small-sample/cache-friendly bias by testing the full key set in random order; this is a first-party benchmark by the library author (Daniel Lemire), not third-party, but code/hardware/build are all public and reproducible so it clears the tier-A bar. Baseline is Go's own map, not C++ std::unordered_map, so this is evidence for the algorithm/language-analogue, not a direct C++ stdlib beat.

name: fastconstmap
workload: 1,000,000 string keys looked up once each in random order (single lookups), plus batched get_many_into over 2000x2000 key batches (cold and hot cache) via a CPython C-extension binary-fuse-filter static map.
claimed_speedup: Single lookup: 95.2 ns/op vs dict 336.1 ns/op (~3.5x); batched cold: 14.2 ns/op vs 148.7 ns/op (~10x); batched hot: 6.1 ns/op (~24x); memory 9.04 bytes/key vs dict's 118.38 bytes/key (~13x)
compiler_and_flags: C11, -O3 (non-Windows) / -O2 (/O2 on Windows) per setup.py; benchmark scripts public under benchmarks/
hardware: Apple M4 Max; also Intel Xeon Gold 6548N for batched comparisons
tradeoffs: Immutable static map only: all keys must be known before construction, unusable as a general drop-in for dict where keys are added/removed at runtime. C core with a Python C-extension wrapper, so overhead/benefit differs when called from pure C vs through the Python API; author notes single-lookup numbers are dominated by Python call overhead, not raw map cost.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the library author (Daniel Lemire); compares against Python's built-in dict, not std::unordered_map, so it is evidence for the binary-fuse-filter static-map technique (usable from C++ via its C API) rather than a direct C++ stdlib beat. Same author/technique family as lemire/constmap (Go) and an unreleased-on-HN lemire/rsconstmap (Rust); only the ones actually surfaced on HN are reported here.
found_via: Hacker News: comment by zahlman on story "Python sets and dictionaries can have quadratic-time performance" (query "perfect hash", tags=comment) linking https://pypi.org/project/fastconstmap/
